items.title: [RFC]: Derive KV offload save sources from prefix-cache records
items.body:
### Motivation.

Two related changes are proposed for KV connector save paths:

1. Derive offload sources from prefix-cache records for every KV-cache group instead of resolving a physical block positionally from a connector-owned copy of the request block table.
2. For connectors using this path, allow saving only when prefix caching is enabled and produces validated content keys.

Together, these make one correctness argument cover both systems: if the GPU prefix cache says a physical block holds a particular prefix hash, KV offload may save that block under that key.

This is narrower than the general offloading architecture in #19854 and the multi-tier design in #38260. It concerns how a save identifies the bytes belonging to a content key.

Several public fixes expose parts of the same invariant:

| PR | Relevant invariant |
|---|---|
| #51358 | Save exact core-selected Mamba boundary states rather than resolving them positionally |
| #51766 | Preserve running-request Mamba CoW ownership after external hits |
| #52372 | Keep GPU blocks referenced while asynchronous Mooncake store jobs read them |
| #43468 | Publish self-describing offload events |
| #44784 | Make MTP/EAGLE offloading lifecycle safe |
| #46972 | Store interior chunk-boundary blocks under MTP/EAGLE |
| #48596 | Save final blocks and prevent reuse races |
| #49671 | Defer request finalization until the final store completes |

These changes are useful and should be kept. The RFC asks whether the underlying save-source contract should be made content-addressed across cache groups so correctness does not depend on connector-specific exclusions and positional bookkeeping.

#### Root cause

A positional save typically has this shape:

```python
block_idx = start // block_size
block_id = block_ids_per_group[group_idx][block_idx]
```

That is valid only while logical position to physical block is a stable, total mapping.

It holds for a conventional full-attention block table. It does not generally hold for hybrid cache managers:

- Mamba managers may null and free superseded interior state blocks, relocate speculative scratch blocks, and move a durable partial-tail hash to a CoW destination.
- Sliding-window attention releases head-prefix blocks as the window advances.
- A connector-side mirror or append log does not necessarily observe in-place nulling, freeing, reuse, or CoW movement.

A stale physical ID can therefore refer to another request's live bytes while the save still uses a valid prefix hash. Deduplicating backends can preserve that bad value because a later correct save sees the key as already present.

Per-group exclusions contain known cases but leave the same trap for the next hybrid layout. The desired invariant is stronger: the source block and content key should come from the same cache transition.

### Proposed Change.

#### 1. Record save candidates at prefix-cache insertion

Every path that makes a block reachable under a hash funnels through `BlockPool._insert_block_hash`, including the operations used by:

- `cache_full_blocks` for block-aligned boundaries;
- `cache_partial_block` for sub-block entries;
- `move_block_hashes` for CoW re-pointing.

When recording is armed for a cache group, produce a self-contained entry such as:

```text
(request_id, group_id, block_id, num_tokens, block_hash/content_key)
```

The connector consumes those records instead of reconstructing either the physical source or content key from positional request snapshots.

Recording at the cache insertion boundary has several useful properties:

- It inherits the prefix cache's reachability, retention, and null filtering.
- A recycled block fails closed: reuse resets or replaces its hash binding, so a stale record can be rejected before pinning.
- Full attention, sliding-window attention, and Mamba use the same handoff contract.
- The request ID becomes a routing/lifecycle label rather than the source of truth for content identity.

Durability remains a property of the producer transition. Two examples:

- An append-only attention block or an off-table checkpoint whose model write has completed can be recorded when its hash is inserted.
- A live Mamba partial-tail block must not be offered while the next forward can overwrite it. Record the durable CoW destination when the hash is re-pointed instead.

Before accepting a record, verify that the block still holds the recorded hash. Once accepted, pin the physical block and release it only after all required ranks report the store attempt terminal. Success, deduplication, pressure drop, cancellation, and failure are all terminal for lifetime purposes; a failed save remains a future cache miss rather than a reason to retain an unbounded pin.

Recording should be explicitly armed by a producer connector and scoped per cache group so unused records cannot accumulate.

#### 2. Saves become record-driven; loads remain positional

A load asks where incoming bytes should be written. The request's newly allocated block table is the correct destination address, so loads should remain positional.

A save asks which physical block currently holds the content named by a key. That is a content lookup, so saves should be record-driven.

This distinction also makes pinning and retry semantics explicit:

- The connector pins exactly the blocks it accepts.
- A preempted request's unaccepted records can be dropped.
- Accepted records survive request completion or preemption as long as the hash binding remains valid.
- Retry can be bounded within a handoff without keeping unrelated later blocks pinned behind a token watermark.

#### 3. Require prefix caching for the record-driven save path

With prefix caching disabled, no prefix-cache hash binding exists to validate a save record. The record-driven path should therefore not save.

This is intended as a correctness rule for connectors migrated to this path, not an assumption that every existing offload implementation already follows it. The standard `OffloadingConnector`, `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`, LMCache integrations, and other connectors that maintain their own content index need an explicit decision: adopt the same validated record contract, provide an equivalent independent invariant, or remain on their current path temporarily.

#### 4. Migration

A staged migration can remain independently revertible and gated per group:

1. Move Mamba saves to record-driven handoffs, building on the exact-state and lifetime work in #51358.
2. Re-measure correctness, store coverage, streaming latency, and prefix-hit behavior.
3. Move sliding-window groups. This is a correctness step because head-prefix entries are mutable.
4. Move full-attention groups, then remove the positional save-source path and its per-group exclusions.
5. Revisit token-watermark state such as `_saved_offset`; self-contained handoffs may make range-based resume/retry bookkeeping unnecessary.

Full attention is last because its table is genuinely append-only today. Moving it is primarily a uniformity and code-deletion argument.

#### Expected benefits

- One correctness argument: a save is valid only while the prefix cache validates the content-key-to-block binding.
- Unified handling for full attention, sliding-window attention, and Mamba.
- No latent correctness dependency on a connector's stale block-table mirror.
- Well-defined pin/release behavior across asynchronous stores, preemption, failure, and request completion.
- Less connector-specific machinery: positional source resolution, save masks used only for exclusions, and eventually range-watermark retry state can be removed.

#### Open questions

1. What resume behavior must remain for any positional saver while migration is incomplete, and what should replace `_saved_offset`?
2. KV events are currently emitted from particular aligned-save paths. Should events be emitted directly from accepted/completed records so moving a group does not suppress publication?
3. Should `OffloadingConnector`, `SimpleCPUOffloadConnector`, LMCache, and other positional savers adopt the same record type immediately or in separate follow-ups?
4. #51358 already provides exact Mamba handoffs, pinning, cross-rank completion watermarks, and fail-closed behavior. Should its emission site carry a self-contained content key and become the first implementation of this more general contract?
5. Should prefix caching be required globally for saving, or should connectors with an independently validated content index implement an equivalent capability/interface?
6. How should sub-block boundaries be represented so the record is self-describing across groups with different physical block sizes?

### Any Other Things.

The closest existing RFCs are #19854 and #38260. This proposal does not replace either one; it tightens the save-source identity and lifetime contract within those architectures.

Public implementation context: #51358, #51766, #52372, #43468, #44784, #46972, #48596, and #49671.

AI assistance was used to draft this RFC.

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: EngineCore fails to start with ValueError("value too large") when one processed multi-modal item exceeds mm_processor_cache_gb
items.body:
## Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```
OS                : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64)
Python            : 3.12.3
PyTorch           : 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA runtime      : 13.0.88
Nvidia driver     : 580.126.20
GPU               : NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB)
vLLM              : 0.27.2rc1.dev193+gaa9903490 (nightly image for aa9903490)
```

Code paths are unchanged on current main (verified at 7ddb50788).

</details>

## 🐛 Describe the bug

`cachetools.Cache.__setitem__` raises `ValueError("value too large")` when a
single item is bigger than the cache's entire `maxsize`. The multi-modal
processor caches (`vllm/multimodal/cache.py`) insert processed items without
guarding against this, so any configuration where one processed multi-modal
item exceeds `mm_processor_cache_gb` turns into a hard failure instead of an
uncached item.

The worst case is memory profiling: the profiling dummy is by construction the
maximum-size item, so if the model's max item is larger than the cache, the
engine cannot even boot. Hit in practice with the Qwen3.8 model card's "Long
Video Understanding" recipe (video pixel budget 469,762,048, a processed
max-size video item is several GiB) and the default `mm_processor_cache_gb=4`:

```
(EngineCore pid=520) ERROR [core.py:1346] EngineCore failed to start.
...
  File ".../vllm/multimodal/processing/processor.py", line 1650, in _cached_apply_hf_processor
  File ".../vllm/multimodal/processing/processor.py", line 1531, in _merge_mm_kwargs
  File ".../vllm/multimodal/cache.py", line 392, in get_and_update_item
  File ".../cachetools/__init__.py", line 299, in __setitem__
  File ".../cachetools/__init__.py", line 81, in __setitem__
    raise ValueError("value too large")
ValueError: value too large
```

Raising `--mm-processor-cache-gb` (e.g. to 24) works around it, but the error
gives no hint that the cache size is the problem, and an item bigger than the
whole cache can never be a cache hit in the first place — evicting the entire
cache to fail the insert is lose/lose.

Expected behavior: items larger than the cache capacity are served uncached
(with a warning suggesting `mm_processor_cache_gb`), and the engine boots.

Reproduction sketch (any oversized item does it; no GPU needed to see the
raise itself):

```python
import torch
from vllm.multimodal.cache import MultiModalCache

cache = MultiModalCache.get_lru_cache(0.000001, object)   # ~1 KiB
cache["big"] = torch.zeros(4096, dtype=torch.uint8)        # 4 KiB
# ValueError: value too large
```

End to end: serve `Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8` with the model card's long-video
`video_preprocessor_config.json` (`size.longest_edge: 469762048`) and default
`mm_processor_cache_gb`; boot dies with the traceback above.

I have a working fix that routes the three insert sites through a size guard
(deterministic by item size, so the P0 metadata shadow and P1 receiver caches
stay coherent — oversized items are simply always resent with data):
https://github.com/dkrisman/vllm/commits/fix/mm-cache-skip-oversized
Happy to open it as a PR.

items.title: [Bug]: --mm-processor-kwargs cannot scope an override to one modality: videos_kwargs is ignored by profiling while a flat "size" leaks into the image budget (Qwen3-VL)
items.body:
## Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```
OS                : Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS (x86_64)
Python            : 3.12.3
PyTorch           : 2.13.0+cu130
CUDA runtime      : 13.0.88
Nvidia driver     : 580.126.20
GPU               : NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB)
vLLM              : 0.27.2rc1.dev193+gaa9903490 (nightly image for aa9903490)
```

Code paths are unchanged on current main (verified at 7ddb50788).

</details>

## 🐛 Describe the bug

The Qwen3.8 / Qwen3-VL model card's "Long Video Understanding" recipe raises the
**video** processor's pixel budget (`size.longest_edge` from 25,165,824 to
469,762,048, i.e. ~12K to ~224K video tokens). The natural way to apply a
processor override in vLLM is `--mm-processor-kwargs`, and per the review
guidance in #52754, that flag is meant to correspond directly to what the HF
processor accepts. The HF processor does accept a modality-scoped form:
`Qwen3VLProcessor._merge_kwargs` honors
`videos_kwargs={"size": ...}` and applies it to videos only (verified against
transformers 5.x). But vLLM cannot express this override safely in either form:

1. **Scoped form is silently ignored by vLLM's own reads.**
   `--mm-processor-kwargs '{"videos_kwargs": {"size": ...}}'` passes CLI
   validation and reaches the HF processor call (it survives the
   `allow_var_kwargs` filter in `call_hf_processor`), but every place vLLM
   consults mm kwargs itself — `get_max_video_tokens`, the dummy-input builder,
   the data parser's per-item size overrides in `qwen3_vl.py` — only reads the
   flat namespace. Result: encoder-cache profiling reserves for a ~12K-token
   max item while runtime processing can legitimately produce ~229K-token
   items. That is the known under-reservation failure class (encoder cache
   starvation / livelock, cf. #51603).

2. **Flat form leaks across modalities.** `--mm-processor-kwargs '{"size":
   {"longest_edge": 469762048, ...}}'` does lift the video budget, but the same
   flat key is read by the image paths and passed to the image processor, so
   the maximum image item goes from ~16K to ~448K tokens. Observed at boot:

   ```
   Encoder cache will be initialized with a budget of 458752 tokens, and profiled with 1 image items of the maximum feature size.
   ```

   Profiling then runs a 448K-token image dummy through the vision encoder
   (grinds for minutes, and with the default processor cache it aborts boot,
   see #52835).

So the only working way to apply the model card's own recipe today is to edit
`video_preprocessor_config.json` inside the cached checkpoint, which is not
reproducible from serve config and silently reverts on re-download.

### Reproduction (CPU-only, no GPU needed)

```python
from vllm.config import ModelConfig
from vllm.multimodal import MULTIMODAL_REGISTRY

def probe(mm_kwargs, label):
    mc = ModelConfig(model="Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B-FP8", mm_processor_kwargs=mm_kwargs)
    info = MULTIMODAL_REGISTRY.create_processor(mc).info
    v = info.get_max_video_tokens(seq_len=500000, mm_counts={"video": 1, "image": 1})
    print(label, "video =", v, "image =", info.get_max_image_tokens())

probe(None, "stock")
probe({"videos_kwargs": {"size": {"longest_edge": 469762048, "shortest_edge": 4096}}}, "scoped")
probe({"size": {"longest_edge": 469762048, "shortest_edge": 4096}}, "flat")
```

Output on aa9903490:

```
stock   video = 12288    image = 16384
scoped  video = 12288    image = 16384    <- scoped override ignored
flat    video = 229376   image = 458752   <- image budget contaminated
```

Expected: the scoped row should read `video = 229376, image = 16384` (matching
what the HF processor itself would do with the same kwargs), and profiling
should agree with runtime processing.

I have a working fix that overlays HF-style `<modality>s_kwargs` onto the flat
namespace at each of Qwen3-VL's mm-kwargs read sites (flat kwargs keep their
current shared-namespace behavior):
https://github.com/dkrisman/vllm/commits/feat/mm-kwargs-modality-scoped
With it, the probe above returns `video = 229376, image = 16384` for the scoped
form. Happy to turn it into a PR if this direction is acceptable, or to discuss
a generic (non-model-specific) resolution layer instead.

items.title: [Bug]: GLM-5.2 MTP accepts 0% of drafts on MI355X (gfx950); disabling expert parallelism hits hipErrorIllegalAddress
items.body:
### Your current environment

`collect_env.py` output isn't available (the nodes were tied up); details taken from the container image and run logs:

```
vLLM       : 0.27.1+rocm723
PyTorch    : 2.11.0+gitd0c8b1f
ROCm       : 7.2.3
Container  : vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.27.1
GPU        : 8x AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950)
amdgpu     : 6.16.13, kernel 6.8.0-137-generic
Model      : amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 (quark MXFP4)
MoE backend: aiter
```

### 🐛 Describe the bug

GLM-5.2 MTP starts fine on MI355X and then accepts **zero** draft tokens. Speculative decoding is pure overhead — it drafts at ~40-230 tok/s and accepts none of it.

```bash
export VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=1

vllm serve /models/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \
  --served-model-name amd/GLM-5.2-MXFP4 \
  --trust-remote-code \
  --async-scheduling \
  --distributed-executor-backend mp \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.80 \
  --max-model-len 262144 \
  --max-num-seqs 2 \
  --moe-backend aiter \
  --compilation-config '{"mode":3,"cudagraph_mode":"FULL_AND_PIECEWISE"}' \
  --tool-call-parser glm47 --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3}'
```

Startup resolves as expected — target `GlmMoeDsaForCausalLM`, draft `DeepSeekMTPModel` — then:

```
SpecDecoding metrics: Mean acceptance length: 1.00, Accepted throughput: 0.00 tokens/s,
Drafted throughput: 37.80 tokens/s, Accepted: 0 tokens, Drafted: 378 tokens,
Per-position acceptance rate: 0.000, 0.000, 0.000, Avg Draft acceptance rate: 0.0%
```

What I tried:

| # | change | result |
|---|---|---|
| A | as above | `acceptance length 1.00`, per-position `0.000, 0.000, 0.000` |
| B | `num_speculative_tokens: 1` | `acceptance length 1.00`, per-position `0.000` |
| C | `--kv-cache-dtype auto` | `acceptance length 1.05`, per-position `0.046, 0.000, 0.000` |
| D | drop `--enable-expert-parallel` | crashes, see below |

B rules out the startup warning's explanation:

```
WARNING [speculative.py:912] Enabling num_speculative_tokens > 1 will run multiple times
on same MTP layer, which may result in lower acceptance rate
```

Position 0 is 0.000 at `num_speculative_tokens=1` too, so re-running GLM-5.2's single nextn layer isn't what's breaking this — the very first draft token is never accepted.

C says fp8 KV contributes but isn't the cause: bf16 KV lifts position 0 from 0.000 to ~0.05, still far from usable.

D, without expert parallelism, dies during memory profiling instead:

```
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'c10::AcceleratorError'
Search for `hipErrorIllegalAddress' in https://rocm.docs.amd.com/projects/HIP/en/latest/index.html
Exception raised from ~CUDAGraph at /app/pytorch/aten/src/ATen/hip/HIPGraph.cpp:302
```

I also checked whether the unquantized nextn layer is being mis-handled by the quark loader — it isn't, as far as I can tell. Layer 78 is genuinely unquantized in this checkpoint (789 `.weight`, 0 `.weight_scale`, 781 entries in `quantization_config.exclude`), but `DeepSeekMTPModel` sets `mtp_start_layer_idx = num_hidden_layers` and names it `model.layers.78`, which is what the exclude patterns match on. So the exclusions should apply.

For reference, SGLang on the same node with the same checkpoint gets a working draft:

```
Decode batch, #running-req: 1, ..., accept len: 3.00, accept rate: 0.67, cuda graph: True
```

This may be the same root cause as #48568 (MI300X / gfx942), which points at MTP's `mtp_block` reduce-scattering under `--enable-expert-parallel` with TP>1 while the predictor layer doesn't restore full tokens. Filing separately because the symptom here is different in a way that matters: on gfx950 there's no hang and no error — it silently produces a 0% acceptance rate, so a benchmark run looks healthy and just reports worse numbers. Disabling EP also fails differently (illegal address rather than working around it).

Happy to run further diagnostics on gfx950 if that helps.

items.title: Scheduler.schedule() is the most complex function in the codebase (complexity 136, 841 lines)
items.body:
### Your current environment

vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py, schedule() at line 476, handles token budgeting, encoder budget, DP prefill balancing, pause-state checks, speculative decoding, and preemption all in one method. The comment above it explains this is intentional, the algorithm is meant to generalize across chunked prefills, prefix caching, speculative decoding, and future features like jump decoding, so this isn't a surprise so much as a natural consequence of that design.

Given how central this path is (it runs every scheduling step) and how much has landed in it, might be worth a pass to see if any of these concerns (DP prefill balancing, encoder budget tracking) can be split into smaller collaborator methods, mainly for testability as more scheduling policies get added.

items.title: [RFC]: Hybrid SSM models and last-block-replay with SpecDec and APC enabled
items.body:
### Motivation.

Long name, I know, but it should explain the issue we're facing.
Currently, when running a model with EAGLE-like speculative decoding (EAGLE/MTP/DFlash/DSpark) and APC enabled, on prefix cache match, vLLM needs to re-run the last full block of the cached prefix, as the drafter needs access to the first uncached token's EAGLE intermediate states.
This is usually fine for pure attention models, where a block consists of ~16 tokens. For hybrid SSM/attention models, however, each block may contain thousands of tokens (for Nemotron 3 Nano in TP1 it's 4224 tokens per block), and re-running a block can really hurt performance.

This RFC aims to offer a few different possibilities for properly solving this issue.

### Proposed Change.

We came up with three different ideas, and have working prototypes of them, and are actively working on a fourth one, initially rejected as too wasteful, but it might turn out to be the simplest. The ideas can potentially compliment each other, too, and work in unison, which may lead to better performance. We'll validate that once we land on an agreed path forward. The exception here are the last two ideas, both looking at caching the intermediate EAGLE states, just in differing ways.

From least to most involved, the ideas are:

- Partial match block promotion
  - Building on top of @ZJY0516 's work in [#45702](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/45702).
  - First prefix cache hit will re-run last full block, up to `prefix-match-unit` tokens from the end of the block.
  - The SSM state at that point will get promoted, and saved to the prefix cache as a new block.
  - Subsequent matches can match on the new block, and only re-run the last `prefix-match-unit` tokens, with COW so that the prefix cache remains valid in the partial block.
  - Partial block granularity is not limited to "`prefix-match-unit` tokens from the end", specifically, but rather any multiple of `prefix-match-unit` can become a promotion junction.
- Next-token receipt on cached blocks
  - Each cached block will store additional information on the token that was generated following it.
  - If the prefix cache is hit, with the uncached token matching the first token that will be computed, the full prefix cache can be used, without any re-computation needed.
  - Still not sure on this point, but we're working to verify it as well.
- Cache boundary EAGLE states
  - After determining an SSM cache block's size, it is rounded up in number-of-tokens terms for the KV cache, and any diff is used as padding in the SSM view of the block.
  - We can take advantage of that, and before rounding up, append enough memory to the SSM cache for a single token's worth of EAGLE states.
    - For Nemotron 3 Nano in TP1, for example, 5,376 bytes are needed for the EAGLE states, which fits inside the existing `all`-mode APC's padding.
  - These states can then be used in conjunction with the cache, and eliminate the need to re-compute that block altogether.
  - This solution can add quite a lot of code complexity, surrounding different parallelization schemes.
    - With PP, for example, the SSM cache the EAGLE states are written to might belong to a rank that doesn't hold the drafter model.
- Sparse EAGLE cache
  - This is the newly revived idea, and is not fully fleshed or tested yet.
  - Building on top of the existing `HiddenStateCacheSpec`, adapting it for our needs.
  - Only cache states at block boundaries, packing multiple such states into a single cache page and sharing them across requests.
  - Requires somewhat complex bookkeeping:
    - Coupling states with the right prefix
    - Evicting states only when corresponding prefix cache blocks are evicted
    - Consolidating sparse pages as states get evicted

### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

@benchislett @ZJY0516 @yewentao256 @Naveassaf @amitz-nv @amirkl94 @shaunkotek 

### Any Other Things.

_No response_

items.title: [Bug]: PD Multi Tier supplies nothing when the producer already holds the blocks
items.body:
### Summary

In the PD Multi Tier flow (`remote_decoder` / `remote_prefiller`, secondary tier
of `type: p2p`),
a producer that **already holds the requested blocks** supplies nothing to the
consumer. The consumer's fetch demand parks unsatisfied, waits out
`_LOAD_TIMEOUT_S = 30.0`, aborts, and recomputes the prompt locally.

The effect is inverted from the intent: the better the producer's prefix cache
works, the more often the Multi Tier path fails to deliver.

### Environment

- vLLM `v0.27.1`, stock `docker.io/vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1`
- `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, TP=1, `--block-size 128`,
  `--no-disable-hybrid-kv-cache-manager`, `PYTHONHASHSEED=0` on all instances
- 2x H200, RDMA between pods
- Connector on both instances:

```
--kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"OffloadingConnector","kv_role":"kv_both",
  "kv_load_failure_policy":"recompute",
  "kv_connector_extra_config":{"spec_name":"TieringOffloadingSpec",
    "cpu_bytes_to_use":107374182400,"block_size":128,"eviction_policy":"lru",
    "offload_prompt_only":false,
    "secondary_tiers":[{"type":"p2p","host":"$(POD_IP)","port":7777}]}}'
```

Two files (`tiering/p2p/session/server.py`, `.../client.py`) carried added
`logger.info` counters only, no behavioural change; the timings and byte counts
below come from vLLM's own metrics and logs.

### Reproducer

Two instances, A (producer) and B (consumer). No P/D topology, router or proxy
required — three HTTP calls.

1. **Producer leg** on A: `POST /v1/completions`, `max_tokens=1`,
   `kv_transfer_params={"remote_decoder":{"kv_request_id":ID}}`
2. **Consumer leg** on B: `POST /v1/completions`,
   `kv_transfer_params={"remote_prefiller":{"kv_request_id":ID,"remote_host":A,"remote_port":7777}}`

Run that pair twice with a **unique prompt each time** (so the consumer is always
cold). Before the second pair, send the prompt to A once on its own with no
`kv_transfer_params`, so A already holds the blocks.

Prompt ~8K tokens. Watch `vllm:kv_offload_load_bytes_total` on B.

### Observed

| case | producer leg | consumer leg | consumer bytes loaded |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| A cold for the prefix | 0.20 s | 0.16 s | +268,959,744 (256 MiB) |
| A pre-warmed | 0.03 s | **32.9 s** | **0** |

Identical with a real P/D pair (prefill producer, decode consumer):
0.086 s / +256 MiB cold vs 30.2 s / 0 bytes warm. Reproduces every time.

Consumer log for the warm case:

```
P2PSession <A>:7777: <id> round=0 timed out, sending abort
P2PSession <A>:7777: load request <id> (job_id=N) timed out; load job completed
with failure. If this recurs, ensure PYTHONHASHSEED is set to the same value on
all nodes.
```

`PYTHONHASHSEED=0` was set and verified identical on every instance, so that
hint is misleading for this failure mode.

### Analysis

Supply for a PD round can only come from that request's store jobs
(`session/server.py` `_OutboundRequestState.add_stored_blocks`). A warm producer
creates no store job, so demand parked in `demanded`
(`key -> remote_block_idx: blocks peer wants, awaiting supply`) is never matched.

Two gates prevent the blocks from being offered:

1. `distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py` (~L941):

```python
# Skip prefix-hit chunks for block-level policy; for
# request-level, next_stored_chunk_idx stays at 0 so all
# chunks (including hits) are offloaded.
if req_status.offloading_context.policy == OffloadPolicy.BLOCK_LEVEL:
    group_state.next_stored_chunk_idx = num_chunks
```

`P2PTierManager.on_new_request` returns a bare `RequestOffloadingContext()`,
which defaults to `BLOCK_LEVEL`. `grep -c REQUEST_LEVEL` is **0** for every tier
(`p2p`, `fs`, `obj`, `example`) at `v0.27.1` **and on `main`**, so
`request_level_tiers` is always empty and
`TieringOffloadingManager._cascade_existing_blocks_to_request_level_tiers` never
runs.

2. Forcing `REQUEST_LEVEL` for producer-side requests clears gate 1 — verified,
the request then reaches the store path with `next_stored_chunk_idx=0` and 56
storable chunks — but the keys are then dropped by `if block_id == 0: continue`,
since a prefix-hit request has no GPU block ids recorded for those blocks
(measured: 55 keys dropped). `new_offload_keys` empties, `prepare_store` is
skipped, and with it the cascade.

### Why symmetric (non-PD) Multi Tier is unaffected

`session/server.py`:

> `# Supply came from inbound lookup pins (symmetric): no late submit_store can arrive, so unmatched fetch demand fails fast. PD rounds park demand for stores instead.`

`session/client.py`:

> `PD-only loads leave probes/unsent empty ... PD clients never probe and stay on round 0.`

The symmetric path supplies from tier lookups and pins, which need neither a store job
nor GPU block ids, so a warm producer is its best case. PD has no equivalent
route.

### Impact at scale

Shared-prefix workload, 8 producers + 8 consumers, 10,800 requests. Supply match
rate tracks producer cache warmth:

| | cold | warming | warm |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| fetch demand matched | 93.8% | 51.5% | **36.7%** |

6,083 load timeouts were logged against 10,800 requests. End to end this made
PD Multi Tier slower than plain NIXL P/D on the same hardware (1571 s vs
1032 s to completion; mean TPOT 92 ms vs 10.7 ms).

### Question

Should the PD Multi Tier path gain a lookup/pin supply route like the symmetric one, or should
the p2p tier declare `REQUEST_LEVEL` (and the store path then be able to offload
prefix-hit blocks that have no GPU block id)? The second looks like it fights both
the `BLOCK_LEVEL` optimisation and the missing block-id constraint, so the first
seems closer to the existing design — but that is your call.

cc @liranschour

items.title: [ROCm][AMD] Kimi-K3 gfx942 / MI325X Gap and Roadmap
items.body:
Sibling of [#50682](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/50682). That tracker is the general Kimi-K3 ROCm roadmap. Most of it is gfx950 / MI355X. This issue is the gfx942 / MI325X (and MI300X) plan on top of current `vllm-project/vllm` main.

gfx942 is already listed as a one-line gap in #50682, with [#50817](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50817) as the enablement PR. The work below should land as stacked PRs on main, not as a private fork.

CC:

- [@xaguilar-amd](https://github.com/xaguilar-amd)
- [@hissu-hyvarinen](https://github.com/hissu-hyvarinen)
- [@jhartika-amd](https://github.com/jhartika-amd)
- [@hongxiayang](https://github.com/hongxiayang)
- [@tjtanaa](https://github.com/tjtanaa)
- [@seanfilimon](https://github.com/seanfilimon)
- [@mpashkovskii](https://github.com/mpashkovskii)
- [@LucasWilkinson](https://github.com/LucasWilkinson)
- [@fxmarty-amd](https://github.com/fxmarty-amd)

## Why gfx942 is a separate plan

Kimi-K3 is 93 layers, 69 KDA + 24 gated MLA, 96 heads. TP8 is 12 heads per rank. The day-0 image and [recipes.vllm.ai Kimi-K3](https://recipes.vllm.ai/moonshotai/Kimi-K3?hardware=mi355x&features=reasoning) target MI355X.

On gfx942 today:

- [#50516](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50516) makes the MXFP4 checkpoint constructible via lossless EMULATION. That path is about 9x to 15x slower than a real quantized MoE kernel, and it does not survive CUDA-graph capture. See the gfx942 measurements on #50682.
- The fused KDA decode kernel from [#50654](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50654) is still gfx950-only in current main. Runtime gate is `on_gfx950()` in `is_fused_kda_decode_supported`. CMake only adds `fused_kda_decode_kernel_rocm.cu` when `gfx950` is in the arch list.
- Gluon MLA decode asserts `mla_gluon requires gfx950` for the 12-head TP8 shape unless the asm pad-to-16 path is used.

## KDA decode fallback is still on main

This is not leftover fork code. On gfx942, current main still runs the unfused KDA decode path: `causal_conv1d_update` + `fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode` + `FusedRMSNormGated.forward_native`. The native gated RMSNorm is `pow` / `mean` / `rsqrt` / `sigmoid` as separate ATen launches. Inductor does not fuse this on ROCm.

Measured on MI325X, TP8, `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE`, `moonshotai/Kimi-K3`, one representative KDA+MoE decode layer. CUDA-graph replay, so these are real launches inside the graph.

KDA decode block only (conv + recurrent + gated output RMSNorm), 16 launches, 74.9 us:

| Step | Launches | Time (us) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `causal_conv1d_update` | 1 | 4.7 |
| `fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode` | 1 | 10.8 |
| `FusedRMSNormGated.forward_native` (`aten::pow`, `mean`, `rsqrt` path, `sigmoid`, copies) | 14 | 59.4 |
| **KDA decode fallback total** | **16** | **74.9** |

That is about 17% of this KDA+MoE layer. There are 69 KDA layers. [#52293](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52293) collapses the same block to one kernel at 7.8 us on gfx942. End-to-end TPOT barely moves until MoE is no longer the emulation path. The fusion is still required. The 14 ATen launches sit on the ~4 us launch floor and will not get cheaper by themselves.

The rest of a KDA+MoE layer is MoE routing, expert GEMM, TP all-reduce, and AttnRes. Those are later waves. The table above is the KDA fusion case.

## Wave 0: make gfx942 a real upstream baseline

Nightly is not a gfx942 baseline until a real MoE kernel and a small-head MLA route exist on main.

1. **AITER pin that includes [ROCm/aiter#4646](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4646).** [#51728](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51728) bumps to `v0.1.19.post2`. That tag is 2026-08-05. aiter#4646 (FlyDSL a16wi4) merged 2026-08-13, so it is not in post2. #51728 is still open, so including 4646 in this bump is still doable. Either retarget #51728 at a SHA after `4bbc57db`, or land post2 and follow immediately with a pin that contains 4646. #50682 already lists 4646 under the AITER docker upgrade. gfx942 should not wait for a later release if this pin can take it now.
2. **[#50817](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50817).** Native MXFP4 Triton `moe_gemm_a16w4` on gfx942, plus pad-to-16 MLA for 12 heads at TP8. This is the default enablement path. It does not depend on aiter#4646. Reported decode went from the emulation baseline to about 100 tok/s.
3. **Recipes and CI.** A gfx942 recipe on recipes.vllm.ai, and a gfx942 gsm8k / serve job on the public ROCm image. Without that, gfx942 keeps regressing silently.
4. **Load-time INT4 through the online-quant RFC, not extra checkpoints.** See the quantization section below.

## Wave 1: KDA fusion on gfx942

All of this is on top of #50654 / [#52606](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52606), not a second KDA stack.

1. **[#52293](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52293).** Enable the existing fused KDA decode kernel on gfx942. This is the PR that removes the 16-launch block in the table. Do not open a competing o_norm fusion PR.
2. **[#51183](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51183).** Write KDA decode into the layer buffer.
3. **KDA prefill on gfx942.** #52606 is the fused prefill work, currently gfx950-gated. After it lands, a small gfx942 gate PR, same shape as #52293.

## Wave 2: MLA (blocked on open AITER)

K3 MLA is dense gated MLA, NoPE, QK 192 / V 128, 12 heads per rank at TP8. Pad-to-16 in #50817 / [#50578](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50578) is the bridge.

1. [ROCm/aiter#4582](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4582) then draft [#51195](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51195) (native CDNA3 Gluon decode for measured verify shapes).
2. [ROCm/aiter#4645](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4645) then draft [#51551](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51551) (opt-in FP8 D192/V128 prefill).
3. A durable sub-16-head gfx942 decode in AITER, so we do not pad 12 heads to 16 forever.

DSA sparse-MLA kernels (indexer + top-k) do not apply here. K3 is hybrid KDA + dense MLA.

## Wave 3: after MoE is not emulation

Only after Wave 0. Otherwise the e2e signal is noise.

- Latent-MoE all-reduce overlap: draft [#51437](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51437)
- AttnRes follow-ups on top of [#50593](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/50593)
- GEMM / FlyDSL tile work that #50817 still has to runtime-patch

[#52190](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52190) (`torch.compile` for `fused_qk_rmsnorm`) is not the gfx942 KDA o_norm fix.

## Load-time INT4 belongs in the online quantization RFC

[#52167](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/52167) item 4 is "Requantize already-quantized layers to different precision." It already cites draft [#51274](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/51274). That is the right place.

I think that we should not keep publishing extra Hugging Face checkpoints every time a new MXFP4 MoE model needs a gfx942 kernel. That is a bottleneck, and the models will keep coming. Kimi-K3, Qwen3.8, and likely more upcoming MXFP4 MoE models can use one opt-in at-load conversion onto an INT4 expert kernel that AITER already has (groupwise INT4 / a16wi4 once aiter#4646 is in the pin).

#51274 is a Kimi-K3 prototype of that: `--quantization-config.moe.weight int4_per_group_32`, default path unchanged, lossy and explicit. It should be generalized under #52167 rather than cloned per model. It stays draft until the AITER pin contains [ROCm/aiter#4646](https://github.com/ROCm/aiter/pull/4646).

#50817 remains the native MXFP4 gfx942 path. Load-time INT4 is the opt-in when that kernel is missing or slower, not a silent default.

## How to use this issue

Stack PRs on main. For each PR: full gsm8k if it can change text, and `vllm bench serve` with `FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` if it claims perf. Same bar as #50682.

Please comment here with gfx942 PRs so they do not only land on the gfx950 tracker.

AI assistance was used to draft this tracker. I reviewed the plan, the public PR list, and the kernel table.

items.title: [Feature][ROCm] Per-layer-type KV-scale calibration for hybrid models — calibrate full-attention layers only, skip recurrent layers (unblocks fp8 KV on GDN/KimiLinear hybrids)
items.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

#37554 was resolved by **disabling `--calculate-kv-scales` entirely on hybrid models** with recurrent layers (GDN/Mamba/SSM): the calibration pass is unreliable because recurrent state is uninitialized, so scales silently fall back to 1.0.

That fix protects correctness but leaves hybrid models with **no path to usable fp8 KV at all**, because:

1. Scale-1.0 fp8 clips attention outliers. Measured on Kimi-K3 (24 MLA layers + 69 KDA recurrent layers, 8×MI300X): every one of the 24 MLA layers reports `_k_scale_float=1.0 _v_scale_float=1.0` under `fp8_e4m3` (the checkpoint ships no KV scales); at 200k+ context this first showed as coherent-but-wrong long-context retrieval and, on the current ROCm build, a GPU worker death on the first 200k prompt.
2. Static scales (`K_SCALE_CONSTANT` etc.) need a measured abs-max from real long-context activations — which is exactly what the disabled calibration pass would have produced. Chicken-and-egg.
3. On ROCm there is no scale-free escape hatch: `fp8_e5m2` has no attention backend (`No valid attention backend found for rocm`), so e4m3+scales is the only viable fp8 KV.

**The ask:** make KV-scale calibration **layer-type-aware** instead of all-or-nothing. On a hybrid, only the full-attention (KV-cache-bearing) layers need scales — the recurrent layers have fixed-size state and no growing KV cache, and they are precisely the layers that make the current calibration unreliable. Calibrating *only* the attention layers and pinning recurrent layers out of the pass would sidestep the #37554 failure mode entirely.

**Why it matters:** on hybrids the KV cache is small per token but is still the context-length limiter. Concretely, Kimi-K3 on 8×192 GB MI300X: bf16 KV caps at 640k tokens with CUDA graphs; fp8 KV would fit 768k+. Anyone serving GDN-hybrid models (Kimi-K3, Qwen3.5 per #37554) at long context hits this wall.

### Alternatives

- Forcing calibration on (patching out the hybrid check): vLLM's own warning says the resulting scales are unreliable — not shippable.
- Static per-layer scale env vars: blocked on the same missing measurement (see 2 above).
- Offline calibration (e.g. llm-compressor-style KV-scale pass) producing checkpoint scales: works in principle, but doesn't help the (common) case of checkpoints that ship without scales; runtime calibration restricted to attention layers is strictly more general.

### Additional context

Measured artifacts available on request: per-layer scale dump (24 MLA layers × 8 TP ranks, all 1.0), e5m2 backend-selection failure log, e4m3 worker-death log at 200k ctx. Environment: `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:kimi-k3` image (v0.1.dev19253+g5f76ae224), ROCm 7.2.53211, 8×MI300X.

items.title: [Bug][ROCm] Kimi-K3 (KimiLinear/GDN hybrid) + ngram spec-decode: GPU memory access fault on concurrent mixed spec/non-spec batches (single-stream works after fixing a strided `state_indices` slice)
items.body:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>collect_env output (summary; full output attached)</summary>

- vLLM: `0.1.dev19253+g5f76ae224.d20260727` — the official ROCm Kimi-K3 image `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:kimi-k3`, with aiter built from source at `ROCm/aiter@e8f438a748d27d5350b9a2d63c8e1cffc2626f52` (2026-08-17)
- PyTorch: 2.11.0+gitd0c8b1f (ROCm 7.2.53211), Python 3.12.13, Ubuntu 22.04.5
- Hardware: 8× AMD Instinct MI300X (gfx942), single node, TP=8
- Model: `nota-ai/Kimi-K3-Nota-Global-Pruned-25` (MXFP4). Note: expert-pruned K3 variant — the pruning affects MoE expert counts only; the KDA/GDN and MLA attention layers are architecturally identical to stock Kimi-K3, and the files involved in this bug (`vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/third_party/kda/fused_recurrent.py`, `vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/gdn/kimi_gdn_linear_attn.py`, `vllm/v1/attention/backends/gdn_attn.py`) were verified byte-identical to the image's stock copies before testing.

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Enabling ngram speculative decoding on Kimi-K3 (KimiLinear hybrid: 69 KDA/GatedDeltaNet recurrent layers + 24 MLA layers) produces **two distinct failures** on the ROCm build:

**Failure 1 (root-caused, workaround proven): strided `state_indices` rejected by the KDA single-token decode kernel.**

The first decode request after enabling `--speculative-config '{"method":"ngram","num_speculative_tokens":6,"prompt_lookup_max":4,"prompt_lookup_min":2}'` dies on every TP worker:

```
File ".../vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/gdn/kimi_gdn_linear_attn.py", line 609, in _forward
    core_attn_out_non_spec, _ = fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode(
File ".../vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/third_party/kda/fused_recurrent.py", line 564, in fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode
    raise ValueError("`state_indices` must be contiguous and one-dimensional.")
```

Diagnostics show `state_indices` arrives as **ndim=1, shape=(1,), stride=(7,)** — a strided column-slice of the block table (`block_table_tensor[~spec_mask, 0]`, row-stride = num_speculative_tokens+1 = 7). Without spec-decode the mask is all-true and the slice comes out contiguous, which is why only the spec path trips it. The data itself is correct (one read-only state-slot index per request); only the layout is strided, so a compacting copy is lossless:

```python
# fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode, before the strict guard:
if state_indices.ndim != 1 or state_indices.stride(0) != 1:
    if state_indices.ndim == 1:
        state_indices = state_indices.contiguous()   # <- fix
    else:
        raise ValueError("`state_indices` must be contiguous and one-dimensional.")
```

With this in place, **single-stream ngram spec-decode works and is a large win**: mean acceptance length 5.45/5.41/4.80 (num_spec=6), accepted throughput up to **33.8 tok/s** vs 25.7 tok/s baseline on retrieval-shaped prompts, output exactness verified at temp=0 against a 200k-context needle suite (50/50 facts, identical to non-spec).

**Failure 2 (the blocker, unresolved): GPU memory access fault under concurrent mixed spec/non-spec batches.**

With the workaround in place, running **≥8 concurrent requests** through the same server GPU-faults all 8 devices within ~a minute:

```
Memory access fault by GPU node-7 (Agent handle: 0x15c8c3d0) on address 0x73862f600000. Reason: Unknown.
Memory access fault by GPU node-9 (Agent handle: 0x170d4d00) on address 0x7210ff200000. Reason: Unknown.
... (all 8 GPUs)
GPU core dump failed
(EngineCore pid=543) ERROR ... Worker proc VllmWorker-2 died unexpectedly (exit code: None), shutting down executor.
```

The fault correlates with batches that mix spec-accepted and non-spec requests (the spec-decode metrics immediately before the fault show acceptance collapsing as the batch mixes). Our read: the concurrent spec+non-spec KDA recurrent-state indexing walks state out of bounds — the single-request `.contiguous()` read is benign, but the multi-request spec path has a deeper state-indexing bug. We deliberately stopped patching at this point (GPU-fault-class bugs are yours to own, not something downstream should whack-a-mole).

### Repro

```bash
# image: vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:kimi-k3  (+ aiter main built from source, see env)
python3 -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model nota-ai/Kimi-K3-Nota-Global-Pruned-25 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 --max-model-len 655360 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 --max-num-seqs 64 --block-size 128 \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --language-model-only --trust-remote-code \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"ngram","num_speculative_tokens":6,"prompt_lookup_max":4,"prompt_lookup_min":2}'
# env: VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MLA=0 HSA_ENABLE_IPC_MODE_LEGACY=0
#      VLLM_ROCM_QUICK_REDUCE_QUANTIZATION=FP NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0
#      PYTORCH_HIP_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:False
```

1. Single `/v1/completions` request → Failure 1 (ValueError) on stock code; works with the `.contiguous()` workaround at 33.8 tok/s accepted throughput.
2. 8+ concurrent `/v1/completions` requests (mixed lengths) → Failure 2 (GPU memory access fault, all devices) within ~1 minute.

### The question for maintainers

Since our image was built (2026-07-27), this exact path has been reworked on main: #50649 *"Fix KDA NaN on mixed batches and racy autotune config"*, #50654 *"Fused kernel for KDA decode"*, #51862 *"Remove prefill pipeline stall in chunk KDA"* — and `kimi_gdn_linear_attn.py` now materializes the non-spec batch via `index_select` (which would also fix Failure 1 by construction).

- **Does the current main/next kimi-k3 ROCm image fix the concurrent mixed spec/non-spec KDA fault (Failure 2)?** #50649's NaN fix touches mixed batches but the symptom we see is an OOB fault, not NaN.
- If it's believed fixed, we're happy to validate a new `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:kimi-k3` (or nightly rocm) image on our 8×MI300X node and report back — ngram spec is worth ~30% end-to-end on this model and is currently the only spec-decode path that works on gfx942 (draft-model/DSpark and aiter-MLA paths are gfx950-only).

Full logs available: complete ValueError traceback (all 8 workers), the strided-shape diagnostic, spec-decode metrics leading into the fault, and the GPU-fault log. Full bundle (secret gist): https://gist.github.com/skimanwhite/135d50e01ce9da029ba01bdaa4d10ba0

items.title: [Feature][DSpark]: Enable varlen for GLM-5.x/DSV3.2 (Sparse MLA)
items.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Adaptive verification has a firm requirement that the attention backend must not use the CPU-side query lengths as a source-of-truth, instead using the GPU tensors (so that we can run the confidence-based assignment on the GPU without synchronizing the CPU).

Additionally, kernels must be able to support decode batches where requests have different query lengths per request.

GLM-5.x models using DSV3.2-style sparse MLA should be compatible through FlashInfer's SM100 TRT-LLM sparse-MLA kernel. vLLM currently derives the sparse token-to-request mapping from CPU query boundaries, and the target capability check also includes draft attention that is captured by a separate graph manager. We should wire up the device-length path, validate correctness, evaluate performance, and merge support.

items.title: CustomAllreduce admits cross-node TP=2 groups and dies in cudaIpcOpenMemHandle (custom_all_reduce.cuh:143 'invalid resource handle') on MNNVL GB200 NVL72
items.body:
### Your current environment

The environment-collection script could not be run inside the CI job container, so the values below are taken from the job's captured environment.

- Hardware: GB200 NVL72, MNNVL fabric, compute capability 10.0, aarch64 (Neoverse-V2)
- Two nodes, 1 GPU visible per node, TP workers placed by Ray across both nodes
- vLLM `0.27.2rc1.dev150+g311b3513a` (from the published `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` image)
- torch `2.13.0+cu130`, CUDA 13.0.2, driver 580.178.04
- `nccl-cu13` 2.30.7, `flashinfer-python` 0.6.16.post3, `ray` 2.57.0
- Model: an FP8 (ModelOpt) MoE checkpoint, ~120B total / ~12B active parameters

### 🐛 Describe the bug

On a GB200 NVL72 (MNNVL) system, serving with `--tensor-parallel-size 2` where the two TP ranks land on **two different nodes** (one GPU visible per node, Ray-distributed) aborts both ranks during engine-core startup with:

```
Cuda error /workspace/csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:143 'invalid resource handle'
```

Line 143 is the `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle` call in `open_ipc_handle()`. The process dies via `exit(EXIT_FAILURE)` inside `CUDACHECK`, so there is no Python traceback and the server never starts. A `cudaIpcMemHandle_t` is only valid within a single node, so opening a peer's handle across a node boundary can never succeed — the bug is that `CustomAllreduce` is enabled for this group at all.

No flags are needed to trigger this. It reproduces with vLLM's default configuration (`disable_custom_all_reduce=False`, `enforce_eager=False`), with no attention-backend and no MoE-backend overrides.

#### Steps to reproduce

1. On a GB200 NVL72 system, allocate **two** nodes with **one** GPU visible on each.
2. Start a Ray cluster spanning both nodes.
3. `vllm serve <model> --tensor-parallel-size 2 --trust-remote-code` (add `--quantization modelopt` for a ModelOpt FP8 checkpoint). No other flags.
4. Both ranks abort shortly after the checkpoint finishes loading, during KV-cache profiling / CUDA-graph capture.

#### Expected vs actual

**Expected:** vLLM notices the TP group spans nodes and falls back to NCCL for that group — emitting the same kind of "custom allreduce is disabled" warning it already emits for the PCIe-only and no-P2P cases — and the server starts.

**Actual:** `CustomAllreduce` is selected for the cross-node group and aborts the process inside `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle`.

#### Evidence

A/B with **node layout as the only delta** — same image, same checkpoint, same flags, same TP size, run back to back on the same GB200 NVL72 rack:

| Layout | TP | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 nodes x 1 GPU (cross-node) | 2 | **FAIL** — `custom_all_reduce.cuh:143 'invalid resource handle'` on **both** ranks |
| 1 node x 2 GPUs (same-node control) | 2 | starts normally, reaching `Application startup complete` |

Both runs used the published `vllm/vllm-openai:nightly` image with no extra layers. The same-node row is the control that isolates the cross-node axis; the cross-node row is the failure being reported.

An earlier pair of runs with `--attention-backend FLASHINFER` and `--moe-backend flashinfer_cutlass` explicitly set showed the identical split. Those flags turned out to be redundant: on this sm100 target vLLM selects FlashInfer attention (`vllm/platforms/cuda.py:486`) and `FLASHINFER_TRTLLM` Fp8 MoE (`vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/fp8.py:411`) as its **own defaults**, on both legs. So the failure is not conditional on any backend override.

The same workload on a non-MNNVL DGX B200 cluster starts normally, and its log contains neither the `cuda_communicator.py:266` custom-allreduce selection line nor any locality warning — consistent with the mechanism below rather than with a model or checkpoint problem.

Log ordering on the failing leg:

```
vllm/executor/ray_utils.py:329  WARNING  tensor_parallel_size=2 exceeds available GPUs per node; TP workers spread across 2+ nodes   (emitted twice)
vllm/distributed/device_communicators/cuda_communicator.py:266  using CUSTOM all-reduce for group tp:0
...
vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:6816  Profiling CUDA graph memory: PIECEWISE=83, FULL=83
Cuda error /workspace/csrc/custom_all_reduce.cuh:143 'invalid resource handle'
```

vLLM already knows the group is cross-node — Ray warns about it twice — and then enables node-local CUDA IPC for it anyway. No "custom allreduce is disabled" warning is emitted.

#### Analysis

In `vllm/distributed/device_communicators/custom_all_reduce.py` on `main`, `__init__` computes locality up front:

```python
same_node = all(in_the_same_node_as(group, source_rank=0))
self.mnnvl_only = not same_node
```

but **every** disabling guard is gated behind `same_node`:

```python
if same_node and world_size > 2 and not fully_connected:
    logger.warning("Custom allreduce is disabled because it's not supported on more than two PCIe-only GPUs. ...")
    return
if same_node and not current_platform.is_rocm() and not _can_p2p(rank, world_size):
    logger.warning("Custom allreduce is disabled because your platform lacks GPU P2P capability ...")
    return
self.disabled = False
```

A cross-node group skips all of them and reaches `self.disabled = False`. The only cross-node guard is:

```python
if not same_node and not self.mnnvl_multicast_ptr:
    logger.warning("Custom collectives are disabled because this multi-node group does not support MNNVL multicast.")
    self.close(); self.disabled = True
```

On MNNVL, multicast **is** available, so `mnnvl_multicast_ptr` is set and this guard cannot fire. The communicator stays enabled.

`should_custom_ar()` then admits every message via the world-size-2 shortcut, with no locality condition:

```python
if self.world_size == 2 or self.fully_connected:
    return inp_size < self.max_size
return False
```

Note that `_SUPPORTED_WORLD_SIZES = [2, 4, 6, 8, 16]` and that the `world_size > 2` guard above is unreachable at world size 2 — TP=2 is exactly the case with no protection.

Finally, `register_graph_buffers()` exchanges IPC handles and registers every peer's buffer unconditionally; on the C++ side that loops over all `j != rank_` and calls `open_ipc_handle()` -> `cudaIpcOpenMemHandle` with no locality branching, which is the abort at `custom_all_reduce.cuh:143`. The timing matches: the crash lands immediately after CUDA-graph memory profiling.

Two further signals that this configuration was never meant to be admitted:

- The class docstring still asserts "all communicators in this group are in the same node."
- The cross-node branch of the meta-buffer setup does not exchange IPC handles at all — it replicates a rank-local pointer:

  ```python
  else:
      meta_ptr, _ = ops.allocate_shared_buffer_and_handle(ops.meta_size())
      self.meta_ptrs = [meta_ptr] * world_size
  ```

  So the code already knows cross-node IPC pointers are not shareable, while the graph-buffer registration path still tries to share them.

#### Suggested fix

Either disable the communicator for cross-node groups that are not on a genuinely MNNVL-only path — mirroring the existing PCIe-only / no-P2P warnings so users get a clear message and an NCCL fallback — or make `should_custom_ar()` and `register_graph_buffers()` locality-aware so the `world_size == 2` shortcut cannot admit a group whose ranks span nodes.

items.title: [RFC]: Rank-Skew-Aware Collective Attribution for Tensor-Parallel Serving
items.body:
### Motivation. Tensor-parallel traces often report a large amount of GPU time inside all-reduce or another collective. That observation alone does not identify the cause. The interval may contain: - useful data transfer limited by the interconnect/backend; - rank-arrival skew, where an early rank waits for a slower peer; - host dispatch or graph-launch skew before the collective; - additional copies/registration imposed by a selected communicator; or - a correctness failure in which ranks issue different collective sequences. These causes require different remedies. Replacing a collective kernel cannot fix time dominated by peer arrival, while reducing host skew cannot raise a genuinely saturated bandwidth ceiling. vLLM has communicator benchmarks and several collective implementations, but it does not expose a common, request/layer-correlated attribution workflow that combines production traces, a message-size-matched zero-skew baseline, and controlled skew injection. This RFC proposes an opt-in profiling facility and offline report that classify collective cost as transfer-dominated, arrival-skew-dominated, mixed, or inconclusive. It complements, but does not duplicate, TP consensus/deadlock work such as #48720: that RFC detects/recoveries collective-sequence failures; this RFC attributes performance when execution is correct. ### Proposed Change. #### 1. Goals - Assign a stable logical ID to sampled TP collectives. - Record per-rank arrival/enqueue and completion evidence without adding a synchronizing collective to the measured hot path. - Run the same operator/message sizes in an isolated calibration benchmark. - Inject controlled rank delay to learn latency sensitivity to skew. - Produce a causally conservative classification with confidence/evidence. - Point optimization work toward host scheduling, batching/parallel policy, overlap, or communicator/backend changes based on the classification. #### 2. Non-goals - Always-on per-collective production tracing. - A new collective implementation. - Automatically changing NCCL algorithms from one trace. - Treating `collective_duration - arrival_skew` as an exact transfer time. - Detecting/recovering mismatched collective sequences (covered by separate reliability work). #### 3. Trace record Illustrative schema: ```python @dataclass(frozen=True) class CollectiveTraceRecord: run_id: str request_class: str step_id: int layer_id: str collective_ordinal: int group_name: str rank: int world_size: int op: str shape: tuple[int, ...] dtype: str payload_bytes: int backend: str execution_mode: str # eager / compile / cuda_graph host_enqueue_ns: int gpu_begin_ns: int | None gpu_end_ns: int | None ``` `(step_id, layer_id, collective_ordinal, group_name)` must be derived from control flow shared by all ranks, not assigned by a rank-local counter that can silently diverge. Trace artifacts are merged after the run. The profiler must not call an extra all-gather/barrier around each measured collective, because that would manufacture or hide the skew being measured. #### 4. Three-source attribution ```mermaid flowchart TD Prod["Sampled production/profile run
per-rank arrival and collective spans"] Base["Isolated calibration
same op, size, dtype, topology, backend"] Inject["Controlled skew sweep
delay one rank by known intervals"] Join["Join by collective signature"] Features["Derived evidence
arrival spread, zero-skew floor,
throughput headroom, skew sensitivity"] Classify{"Conservative classifier"} Wait["Arrival-skew dominated
reduce host/rank imbalance"] Transfer["Transfer dominated
backend/topology/overlap candidate"] Mixed["Mixed
optimize both / change parallel plan"] Unknown["Inconclusive
collect more evidence"] Prod --> Join Base --> Join Inject --> Join --> Features --> Classify Classify --> Wait Classify --> Transfer Classify --> Mixed Classify --> Unknown ``` Evidence sources: 1. **Production arrival spread.** Difference between earliest/latest rank enqueue/readiness for the same logical collective, after clock calibration where needed. 2. **Zero-skew calibration curve.** Latency/throughput distribution for the exact op, payload, world size, topology, backend, and registration mode under synchronized inputs. 3. **Skew-injection curve.** Repeat calibration while delaying selected ranks by controlled intervals. This establishes how the backend's observed span changes when arrival skew is known. The report should not claim an exact decomposition if clocks or execution mode cannot support it. It can still classify when multiple independent measurements agree. #### 5. Clock and execution-mode handling Same-node phase 1 can use a shared host monotonic clock source plus CUDA/CUPTI timestamps, with startup/end calibration and explicit uncertainty. Multi-node support must estimate clock offsets/drift or rely on profiler data with a documented cross-node time base. CUDA graphs require special handling because Python wrappers run at capture rather than each replay. Supported choices include: - graph-node/CUPTI/Nsight evidence correlated to a deterministic collective ordinal; - sampled eager/compile runs for arrival instrumentation plus a separate graph-mode calibration; or - backend profiler callbacks that execute on replay. The report must label evidence as capture-time or replay-time and must not reuse capture timestamps as though they describe every replay. #### 6. Instrumentation modes Proposed modes: - `off` (default): no records or extra state; - `trace`: short, explicitly profiled run with detailed sampled records and NVTX ranges; - `aggregate`: optional low-rate sampled summaries if a provider can supply replay-safe timestamps without synchronization; and - `calibrate`: isolated communicator benchmark plus optional skew sweep. Instrumentation belongs near `GroupCoordinator`/device-communicator dispatch so custom all-reduce, pynccl, symmetric-memory, and platform providers emit the same schema. High-level `tensor_model_parallel_all_reduce()` can add request/layer context without owning timing. #### 7. Derived report For each collective signature, report: - call count and total payload bytes; - per-rank enqueue spread distribution; - observed collective span/duration distribution; - calibrated zero-skew p50/p95 and achieved bandwidth; - hardware/topology bandwidth ceiling when available; - skew-injection response curve; - backend/algorithm/registration and graph mode; - classification and confidence; - missing evidence/clock uncertainty; and - suggested next experiment, not an automatic configuration change. Example decision logic (thresholds to be validated, not hard-coded by this RFC): - observed latency near zero-skew calibration and bandwidth near measured ceiling -> transfer-dominated; - observed excess latency tracks arrival spread and injected-skew curve while zero-skew calibration has headroom -> arrival-skew-dominated; - both arrival spread and zero-skew transfer cost are material -> mixed; - mismatched op IDs/call counts -> stop performance attribution and route to correctness/consensus diagnostics; - otherwise -> inconclusive. #### 8. Optimization routing The report maps classifications to candidate work: | Classification | Candidate next steps | | --- | --- | | Arrival-skew dominated | profile host dispatch/pre-collective compute, remove rank-asymmetric work, reduce tiny collective fragmentation, evaluate smaller TP | | Transfer dominated | evaluate backend/algorithm/topology, fusion, overlap, payload/layout, or a different parallel axis | | Mixed | address largest source first; rerun attribution after each change | | Inconclusive | improve clock/replay instrumentation or collect a longer isolated trace | This table is guidance, not an auto-tuner. #### 9. Validation Synthetic tests: - zero injected skew with payload sweep; - fixed delay on one rank and alternating delayed rank; - compute imbalance before a collective; - bandwidth saturation with large payloads; - many small collectives dominated by launch overhead; - custom all-reduce registered/unregistered buffers; - eager, compile, and CUDA-graph replay where supported; and - intentionally mismatched collective IDs to verify handoff to reliability diagnostics. Correctness/safety tests: - `off` adds no hot-path allocation or thread; - profiler emits no additional measured-group collectives; - trace collection cannot change collective order; - bounded buffers drop samples with a counter rather than blocking execution; - artifacts exclude prompt/output tensor contents by default; and - profiler teardown works after request cancellation/error. #### 10. Benchmark plan Use the existing device-communicator benchmark as the calibration entrypoint where possible. Add: - exact production payload list import; - controlled pre-call delay per rank; - output JSON matching the trace schema/signature; - at least two TP world sizes and small/large payload regimes; and - comparison across the communicator(s) available on the test topology. Then run one representative model in trace mode and verify that the tool's classification matches the synthetic regime introduced before selected layers. #### 11. Alternatives considered - **Use only Nsight time inside NCCL.** It identifies where time is observed, not why peers entered at different times. - **Use only an isolated NCCL benchmark.** It gives a ceiling/floor but cannot show whether production ranks arrive together. - **Subtract arrival spread from duration.** Collective protocols overlap waiting and transfer nonlinearly; the result is not a reliable exact decomposition. - **Insert barriers around each collective.** This destroys the phenomenon under measurement and adds overhead. - **Reuse the TP consensus guard.** Collective-count health is valuable but does not quantify healthy-run transfer versus skew cost. #### 12. Phased plan 1. Define schema and add skew injection/output JSON to the communicator benchmark. 2. Add `trace` instrumentation for eager same-node TP behind an explicit profiler option. 3. Build the offline join/classification report with uncertainty. 4. Validate against synthetic known-skew and bandwidth regimes. 5. Add compile/CUDA-graph replay evidence. 6. Consider multi-node clock calibration and low-rate aggregate mode separately. ### Feedback Period. At least one week. ### CC List. items.title: [RFC]: Extensible GEMM Epilogue Contracts for Residual, Norm, and Gated Activation Fusion
items.body:
### Motivation. vLLM has mature linear-kernel selection and several compiler fusion passes, but the kernel interface and the graph-fusion interface do not yet share one typed contract for fusing a producer GEMM with adjacent residual, normalization, scaling, quantization, or gated-activation work. Today a provider is generally selected to produce the linear output, after which model code or a compilation pass applies downstream operations. This leaves two recurring gaps: 1. a provider that can evaluate a valid epilogue while accumulators are still in registers cannot advertise that capability through the same selection path; and 2. correctness constraints around reduction domains and tensor-parallel collective boundaries are encoded in one-off fused modules/patterns instead of one fail-closed contract. This RFC proposes an optional `GemmEpilogueSpec` understood by linear-kernel providers and compiler rewrites. It is not a request to fuse every decoder block or to require one backend. A provider may accept a spec only when it can implement the exact shape, dtype, reduction, aliasing, and distributed semantics; otherwise vLLM uses the existing unfused path. The initial target is the common Transformer structure in which GEMMs are interleaved with residual addition, RMSNorm-style normalization, scaling/quantization, and SwiGLU-like gated activations. Diffusion/omni models are a downstream consumer, but the abstraction belongs in vLLM's kernel boundary if it is sufficiently generic. ### Proposed Change. #### 1. Design principles - Optional and fail closed: existing kernels and model paths are unchanged without a matched spec. - Typed semantics, not arbitrary Python callbacks in the hot path. - Provider-neutral: CUTLASS/CuTe DSL, Triton, FlashInfer, vendor plugins, or native code may implement a capability. - Compiler-aware: a graph pass may request a spec only after matching a proven graph. - TP-aware: a row-parallel partial sum cannot be normalized as though it were the complete tensor before all-reduce. - Numerically explicit: accumulation dtype, cast points, reduction dtype, and output/alias semantics are part of the contract. - Measured enablement: a valid fusion is not automatically faster for every shape/batch. #### 2. Proposed types Illustrative API: ```python class EpilogueOp(Enum): BIAS = "bias" RESIDUAL_ADD = "residual_add" ROW_SCALE = "row_scale" RMS_NORM = "rms_norm" STATIC_QUANTIZE = "static_quantize" SILU_MUL = "silu_mul" class CollectiveBoundary(Enum): NONE = "none" PRE_COLLECTIVE_PARTIAL = "pre_collective_partial" POST_ALL_REDUCE_COMPLETE = "post_all_reduce_complete" @dataclass(frozen=True) class GemmEpilogueSpec: ops: tuple[EpilogueOp, ...] accumulation_dtype: torch.dtype output_dtype: torch.dtype reduction_dtype: torch.dtype | None collective_boundary: CollectiveBoundary auxiliary_inputs: tuple[str, ...] outputs: tuple[str, ...] mutates: frozenset[str] class MMLinearKernel(...): @classmethod def can_implement_epilogue( cls, config, spec: GemmEpilogueSpec ) -> tuple[bool, str | None]: ... def apply(self, layer, x, bias=None, *, epilogue=None, **kwargs): ... ``` The final interface may use specialized subtypes rather than an enum list. The important property is that supported compositions are explicit and inspectable. #### 3. Compiler/provider flow ```mermaid flowchart LR Graph["FX/model graph
GEMM + adjacent ops"] Match["Semantic pattern match
shape, alias, reduction, TP boundary"] Spec["Build GemmEpilogueSpec"] Select["Existing linear-kernel selector"] Cap{"Provider can implement
this exact spec?"} Fused["Provider fused GEMM + epilogue"] Fallback["Existing GEMM
+ existing separate ops"] Verify["Debug/CI reference checks
and benchmark gate"] Graph --> Match --> Spec --> Select --> Cap Cap -->|yes| Fused --> Verify Cap -->|no| Fallback ``` Graph matching remains in compilation/model integration. Kernel providers do not parse arbitrary FX graphs. Providers receive a normalized, validated spec. #### 4. Correct placement around tensor parallelism ```mermaid flowchart TD Col["Column-parallel GEMM
output shard is semantically complete
for shard-local eligible epilogues"] Row["Row-parallel GEMM
rank-local partial sums"] AR["Tensor-parallel all-reduce"] Full["Complete output tensor"] Post["Residual / norm / gated op
when reduction domain is complete"] Col --> Post Row --> AR --> Full --> Post ``` Some operations can run on a shard; others require the full hidden dimension or the globally reduced value. The pattern matcher must encode the mathematical reduction domain. A provider cannot accept `POST_ALL_REDUCE_COMPLETE` work on a rank-local partial accumulator. An implementation may eventually fuse all-reduce plus a post-collective epilogue through a communicator/provider that supports it, but that is a separate capability. This RFC must not move normalization across a collective merely to make a kernel shape convenient. #### 5. Initial supported compositions Start small and evidence-driven. Candidate specs: - GEMM + bias; - GEMM + row scale; - GEMM + static output quantization; - GEMM + residual add when aliasing and broadcast semantics are simple; - paired gate/up projections + SiLU-multiply where the provider exposes a joint output contract; and - post-all-reduce residual/RMSNorm only through an existing correctly placed fused collective capability. RMSNorm inside a GEMM epilogue is valid only if the provider can compute the full required row reduction correctly. A tiled GEMM that sees only part of the normalized dimension must reject the spec or use a proven multi-tile reduction scheme. #### 6. Integration with current kernel selection The current `MMLinearKernel` selection lifecycle already separates: - hardware support; - whether a kernel can implement a layer configuration; - parameter processing; and - execution. Add epilogue capability after ordinary layer compatibility. `--linear-backend` continues to constrain providers. A selected backend may still reject a particular epilogue and execute the ordinary linear path; no new backend should be selected solely because it claims a fusion unless the existing priority/benchmark policy allows it. The contract should also be visible in debug logs/metrics: requested spec, selected provider, rejection reason, and fallback path. #### 7. Numerical and aliasing contract Every supported spec declares: - GEMM accumulation dtype; - when the accumulator is cast; - epsilon and reduction dtype for normalization; - whether residual is read before an output write; - exact broadcasting rules for weights/scales/bias; - output dtype(s), including optional dual output; - allowed non-contiguous inputs; and - mutation/alias behavior for `torch.compile` fake/meta implementations. Tests compare against an independent high-precision reference as well as the existing unfused path. A fusion may be numerically closer to the high-precision reference while not bitwise equal to bf16 eager execution; that must be represented by a declared tolerance and model-level gate, not silently treated as exact. #### 8. Validation matrix Unit/kernel tests: - multiple `M/N/K`, including small decode and larger prefill batches; - bf16/fp16/fp8 inputs and supported accumulation/output dtypes; - contiguous and declared non-contiguous layouts; - bias/residual broadcast cases; - alias/mutation checks under eager and `torch.compile`; - negative tests for unsupported reduction domains/spec orderings; - TP world sizes 1/2/4 with a distributed reference; and - graph pass fallback when no provider accepts the spec. End-to-end tests: - at least one autoregressive decoder block; - one diffusion/omni Transformer consumer if the abstraction is shared downstream; - compilation enabled/disabled; and - output/accuracy gates appropriate to the model. #### 9. Benchmark and enablement policy For each provider/spec/shape regime report: - kernel latency and achieved compute/bandwidth; - kernel launch count; - HBM bytes when measurable; - end-to-end latency/throughput; - compile/capture compatibility; - peak workspace memory; and - numerical results. Enable only where end-to-end evidence supports it. A fusion can regress low-batch execution because fixed scheduling/collective overhead outweighs saved launches. The selector/config may need shape-regime gating rather than a universal boolean. #### 10. Alternatives considered - **Keep adding one-off fused modules.** Fast for a single pattern but duplicates capability, fallback, and correctness logic. - **Rely only on compiler-generated fusion.** Valuable and should remain the first option, but does not expose provider-specific GEMM epilogues or distributed placement semantics uniformly. - **Allow arbitrary Python epilogue callables.** Hard to validate, serialize, select, and support across providers. - **Put the abstraction only in vLLM-Omni.** Diffusion is a motivating consumer, but linear-kernel selection and several relevant fusion passes are upstream vLLM concepts. #### 11. Phased plan 1. Agree on the typed spec and rejection/fallback behavior. 2. Implement one minimal existing capability (for example bias/static scaling) through the contract without changing defaults. 3. Connect one compiler pattern and add debug observability. 4. Add distributed-boundary negative/positive tests. 5. Benchmark one residual/norm or gated-activation composition. 6. Let downstream vLLM-Omni/SGLang work evaluate additional providers separately. ### Feedback Period. At least one week. ### CC List. No specific CC requested; feedback from linear-kernel, compilation, distributed, and quantization maintainers would be valuable. ### Any Other Things. Relevant code and discussions: - vLLM linear-kernel interface and providers: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/tree/main/vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear - `MMLinearKernel` base contract: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/base.py - Existing all-reduce/RMSNorm compilation fusion: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/compilation/passes/fusion/allreduce_rms_fusion.py - Hardware-agnostic model-definition RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/44219 - vLLM-Omni diffusion kernel optimization RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/3186 - vLLM-Omni diffusion operator-boundary RFC: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm-omni/issues/5582 - SGLang CUTLASS dynamic epilogue investigation: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/30809 ### Before submitting a new issue... - [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.
